questions.q: A tort is best described as:
o: A breach of a contractual obligation only
A civil wrong (other than breach of contract or trust) for which the remedy is unliquidated damages
Exclusively a criminal offence
A wrong that can only be committed by a government body
questions.src: Tort is a civil wrong distinct from contract/trust breaches, with unliquidated (court-assessed) damages as the typical remedy.

questions.q: "Injuria Sine Damno" refers to a situation where there is:
o: Actual damage but no violation of a legal right — generally not actionable
A violation of a legal right WITHOUT actual damage — which IS actionable
Neither damage nor any legal right violated
Only criminal liability, never civil
questions.src: Injuria Sine Damno means legal injury without measurable loss, and IS actionable since the law protects the legal right itself.

questions.q: "Volenti non fit injuria" as a defence in tort law means:
o: No injury is done to one who consents to a known risk
Every injury must be compensated regardless of consent
Only applies to criminal cases
A defence available exclusively to the government
questions.src: This maxim means a person who voluntarily assumes a known risk cannot later complain of the resulting harm.

questions.q: An employer is generally vicariously liable for the torts of an employee when the tort is committed:
o: At any time, regardless of context
In the course of employment
Only if the employer personally directed the specific act
Never, under any circumstances
questions.src: Vicarious liability attaches for torts committed in the course of employment, not for acts wholly outside its scope ("frolic of their own").

questions.q: In Rylands v. Fletcher (1868), the House of Lords held the defendant liable for the escape of water despite no proven negligence, establishing:
o: The Doctrine of Absolute Liability
The Rule of Strict Liability
The Doctrine of Vicarious Liability
The Rule against Res Ipsa Loquitur
questions.src: Rylands v. Fletcher established the foundational rule of Strict Liability for escape of dangerous things brought onto land.

questions.q: Which of the following is a recognised exception/defence to the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher?
o: The defendant is very wealthy
Act of God, plaintiff's own fault, third-party act, consent, or statutory authority
The escape happened at night
The plaintiff is a corporation
questions.src: These are the recognised categories of exceptions to strict liability under Rylands v. Fletcher.

questions.q: In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987), the Supreme Court held that an enterprise engaged in hazardous activity is:
o: Liable only if negligence is proven
Absolutely liable to compensate for harm, with NONE of the Rylands v. Fletcher defences available
Never liable if it followed government safety regulations
Liable only to government agencies, not private individuals
questions.src: The Absolute Liability doctrine established in M.C. Mehta explicitly excludes ALL Rylands v. Fletcher defences.

questions.q: The key structural difference between Strict Liability and Absolute Liability under Indian law is:
o: They are identical with no difference
Absolute Liability admits no exceptions/defences at all, while Strict Liability has several recognised exceptions
Strict Liability applies only to government bodies
Absolute Liability applies only outside India
questions.src: The defining distinction is the complete absence of any defences under Absolute Liability, unlike Strict Liability.

questions.q: "Battery" as a tort refers to:
o: Merely creating apprehension of contact
Actual, direct, unlawful physical contact/force applied to another person without consent
Only contact occurring in a public place
A tort that can only be committed against property, never a person
questions.src: Battery requires actual unlawful physical contact, distinguished from assault (mere apprehension of such contact).

questions.q: "Malicious Prosecution" as a tort requires proving that criminal proceedings were initiated against the plaintiff:
o: With reasonable and probable cause
Without reasonable/probable cause, with malice, and terminating in the plaintiff's favour
By a government official only
Only where a conviction resulted
questions.src: Malicious prosecution requires absence of reasonable cause, presence of malice, and the underlying proceedings ending favourably for the plaintiff.

questions.q: "Public Nuisance" as distinguished from "Private Nuisance" generally affects:
o: Only one specific individual
The community/public at large, though a private individual with special/particular damage beyond the general public may also sue
Only government property
Only rural areas
questions.src: Public nuisance affects the wider community; a private individual can sue if they suffer special damage distinct from the general public.

questions.q: "Defamation" in the form of a written or permanent statement is called:
o: Slander, requiring proof of special damage
Libel, generally actionable per se without needing to prove special damage
Neither libel nor slander applies to written statements
Assault
questions.src: Libel (written/permanent defamatory statements) is generally actionable per se, unlike slander which usually requires proof of special damage.

questions.q: In Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932), the House of Lords held that a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer:
o: Only if there is a direct contract between them
Even without a direct contractual relationship, based on the "neighbour principle"
Only for food products, never other goods
Only if the consumer is a member of the same household as the purchaser
questions.src: Donoghue v. Stevenson established that duty of care in negligence does not require privity of contract — the neighbour principle governs instead.

questions.q: Lord Atkin's "neighbour principle" from Donoghue v. Stevenson defines a "neighbour" as:
o: Only a person living in physical proximity
Anyone so closely and directly affected by one's act that they ought reasonably to be in contemplation when directing one's mind to the act
Only family members
Only fellow employees
questions.src: The neighbour principle extends duty of care to anyone reasonably foreseeable as affected by one's actions, not merely physical neighbours.

questions.q: The essential elements required to establish the tort of Negligence include:
o: Only proof of damage, nothing else
Existence of a duty of care, breach of that duty, damage caused by the breach, and the damage not being too remote
Only intent to cause harm
Only a written complaint filed with police
questions.src: These four elements — duty, breach, causation, and remoteness — together constitute the tort of negligence.

questions.q: "Passing Off" as a tort against business relations refers to:
o: Filing a false patent application
Misrepresenting one's own goods/business as those of another, exploiting the other's established goodwill
A criminal offence under the IPC only
A tort that applies only to government contracts
questions.src: Passing off protects business goodwill from misrepresentation, a tort with close ties to trademark/unfair competition law.

questions.q: Under the Consumer Protection Act 2019, a person who purchases goods purely for RESALE or commercial purposes is generally:
o: Automatically covered as a "consumer" regardless of purpose
Excluded from the definition of "consumer," subject to a self-employment livelihood exception
Only covered if the goods are expensive
Covered only for services, not goods
questions.src: The Act excludes purely commercial/resale purchases from the "consumer" definition, with a carve-out for goods used for self-employment livelihood.

questions.q: Which of the following is a genuinely NEW feature introduced by the Consumer Protection Act 2019, absent from the earlier 1986 Act?
o: The concept of a "consumer" itself
The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) and a dedicated Product Liability chapter
The right to be heard
District-level consumer forums
questions.src: The CCPA and the Product Liability framework are significant, genuinely new additions under the 2019 Act.

questions.q: In Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995), the Supreme Court held that:
o: Doctors can never be sued under consumer law
Medical services rendered by doctors/hospitals (except free/purely charitable services) fall within "service" under the Consumer Protection Act
Only government hospitals are covered by consumer law
Medical negligence can only be pursued through criminal proceedings
questions.src: This case established that most medical services fall within the Act's definition of "service," allowing patients to approach Consumer Forums for medical negligence.

questions.q: The Consumer Disputes Redressal structure under the 2019 Act consists of how many tiers?
o: Two — State and National only
Three — District, State, and National Commissions
Five, one for each region of India
Only one, a single National Commission
questions.src: The three-tier structure (District, State, National) is based on the value of goods/services and compensation claimed.

questions.q: "Product Liability" under the Consumer Protection Act 2019 allows a consumer to claim compensation for harm caused by a defective product based on:
o: Only manufacturing defects
Manufacturing defect, design defect, or deviation from express warranty
Only the product's price being too high
Only defects discovered within 24 hours of purchase
questions.src: The Product Liability chapter recognises multiple grounds — manufacturing defect, design defect, and warranty deviation — for consumer compensation claims.

questions.q: Motor Vehicle Accident compensation claims in India are typically adjudicated by:
o: Ordinary civil courts exclusively, with no specialised body
Motor Accidents Claims Tribunals (MACT), a specialised body under the Motor Vehicles Act
Only criminal courts
The Supreme Court directly in every single case
questions.src: MACTs are the specialised tribunals established under the Motor Vehicles Act for adjudicating motor accident compensation claims.

questions.q: The doctrine of "Sovereign Immunity" traditionally shielded the State from tort liability for acts done in exercise of:
o: Any function whatsoever, with no distinction
"Sovereign" functions (e.g., defence, legislation), while allowing liability for "non-sovereign"/commercial functions
Only criminal matters
Only matters involving foreign nationals
questions.src: Sovereign immunity traditionally distinguished sovereign functions (immune) from non-sovereign/commercial functions (liable), though this distinction has been increasingly narrowed by modern courts.

questions.q: "Joint Tortfeasors" refers to a situation where:
o: Only one person can ever be sued for a tort
Two or more persons jointly commit a tort causing the same damage, and are jointly and severally liable
Tortfeasors can never be sued together in one action
Joint liability applies only to government employees
questions.src: Joint tortfeasors are jointly and severally liable — the plaintiff may sue any one, some, or all of them for the full amount.

questions.q: "Inevitable Accident" as a defence in tort law refers to an event that:
o: Was intentionally caused by the defendant
Could not have been avoided despite the exercise of reasonable care and skill
Only applies to motor vehicle accidents
Is never a valid defence under any circumstances
questions.src: Inevitable accident is a recognised defence where the harm could not have been prevented despite reasonable care.

questions.q: The Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985 primarily gave:
o: Individual victims sole authority over their own claims, with no government involvement
The Government of India the EXCLUSIVE right to represent all Indian victims in claims against Union Carbide, both in India and abroad
Union Carbide the right to settle claims however it preferred
US courts exclusive jurisdiction over all Bhopal-related claims
questions.src: Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act 1985 — a unique legislative mechanism vesting exclusive representation authority in the Government of India

questions.q: The Supreme Court of India approved a civil settlement of Union Carbide's liability for the Bhopal disaster in 1989 for approximately:
o: USD 4.7 million
USD 470 million
USD 4.7 billion
No settlement was ever reached
questions.src: The 1989 Supreme Court-approved settlement was for USD 470 million, a figure that remained deeply controversial and was later challenged via a 2010 curative petition (which the Court rejected)

questions.q: The Bhopal Gas Tragedy (1984) is understood to have directly influenced the Supreme Court's approach in which subsequent landmark case?
o: Rylands v. Fletcher (1868)
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987, the Oleum Gas Leak case), decided just months after Bhopal
Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932)
Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995)
questions.src: The Bhopal disaster's perceived inadequacy of ordinary strict liability rules directly influenced the Supreme Court's deliberately stricter Absolute Liability doctrine in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, decided in 1987

questions.q: Under the Consumer Protection Act 2019's Product Liability chapter, a 'Manufacturing Defect' refers to:
o: A flaw in the product's overall design affecting the entire product line
A deviation from the product's own manufacturing specifications, arising from a flaw in the production process itself (e.g., one bad batch)
Only defects discovered after 10 years of use
A defect that only applies to imported products
questions.src: Consumer Protection Act 2019 — manufacturing defect is a production-process flaw causing deviation from the manufacturer's own specifications, distinct from a design defect affecting the whole product line

questions.q: Under the Consumer Protection Act 2019, the three recognised grounds for a Product Liability claim are:
o: Only manufacturing defects, with no other grounds recognised
Manufacturing defect, design defect, and deviation from express warranty
Only criminal negligence by the manufacturer
Only defects in imported goods
questions.src: Consumer Protection Act 2019, Sections 82-87 — the three statutory grounds for product liability actions

questions.q: A product SELLER (who is not also the manufacturer) is generally liable for a manufacturing defect under the CPA 2019 only if they:
o: Are automatically liable regardless of any involvement in manufacturing
Exercised substantial control over the manufacturing process, altered/modified the product, or made an independent express warranty
Can never be held liable under any circumstances
Sold the product more than once
questions.src: Consumer Protection Act 2019 — sellers who are not manufacturers face more limited liability, generally requiring substantial control, modification, or an independent warranty
